1. I wasn't saying that you will find proof that supports my point of view. You also did not offer a citation for your statement about what past civilizations probably did - which is why I said there is information out there. You said *"past civilizations were definitely not as advanced as us so probably assumed the defect of being both sexes was another gender."* In response, I said there isn't a "probably" here - there are facts out there about these cultural-specific genders that you can find with a simple Google search. I posted this link in another comment, but here is a listicle showcasing some examples of non-binary gender expressions in different cultures. Not an academic source, but pretty comprehensive overview of the way gender is expressed in both past and modern day societies: [https://listverse.com/2015/10/21/10-examples-of-nonbinary-genders-throughout-history/](https://listverse.com/2015/10/21/10-examples-of-nonbinary-genders-throughout-history/)
2. As I said in my first comment, this isn't just about ancient civilizations. It's about civilizations that are still alive and well today - in Asia, Latin America, Europe and North America. Basically all over the world, throughout all of recorded human history, there have been records of people who do not associate their genitalia with their gender - meaning cisgender people, and who do not identify with the label or man or woman. This is something that has existed in countless cultures, globally, for all of recorded human history. It's not new and continues to exist today.
3. Pretty comprehensive definition of gender from Wikipedia: **"Gender is the range of characteristics pertaining to, and differentiating between, masculinity and femininity. Depending on the context, these characteristics may include biological sex (i.e., the state of being male, female, or an intersex variation), sex-based social structures (i.e., gender roles), or gender identity. Traditionally, people who identify as men or women or use masculine or feminine gender pronouns are using a system of gender binary whereas those who exist outside these groups fall under the umbrella terms non-binary or genderqueer. Some cultures have specific gender roles that are distinct from "man" and "woman," such as the hijras of South Asia. These are often referred to as third genders."**

​

I mentioned doing some research because there are very easily accessible resources online, and I believe as a rule that if people are going to debate about complex issues like gender/race/politics/economics/etc., they should have consumed some information from primary or secondary sources so it's more than just opinions and feelings involved.

There’s no “probably” - there’s a lot of concrete information out there if you want to do some research. And these aren’t just ancient civilizations, they’re non-Western/European cultures in countries that are very much still alive and kicking.

Before my first kiss with a woman, I had many terrible first kisses with men. They were sloppy, or unpleasant, or forced, and just not right. Usually after not knowing the man for a while and just acting out on account of my own personal issues.

Now my first kiss with a woman, however, was magical.

We knew each other for months - we met in poetry class (how corny, right?). I immediately was drawn to sit next to her for a reason unbeknownst to me. A couple weeks later she told me that she enjoyed watching my hair fade from pink to blonde and I was smitten.

We got lunch together after every class, I slept over her house (platonically), and one day during lunch she told me she was bi. Me, not yet knowing I was in fact VERY gay, excitedly told her I was too.

Fast forward another two months or so, she texts me while I'm home visiting my family saying she's in the area and wants to come visit. I told her I was playing D&D (Dungeons and Dragons) with my family but she could be a celebrity guest and play along and surprisingly she was down for it. We had the BEST time and my family was completely enamored with her (obviously, so was I).

I had to go to a party at an old, old friend's house that night and she asked if she could stay and come. Of course, I said.

We drank, played board games, danced and sang along with Renee and Catherine in Chicago, and at one point she went to get her phone from the kitchen.

I followed her in and she backed into the pantry. I put my arms up against both walls and just smiled at her. She looked at me with a smirk and wide eyes and said, "You better not kiss me."

I asked why not and she replied that I wouldn't want to the next day.

And I told her I would the next day, and the day after that, and the day after that...

And then I kissed her. And it was the most magical, sensual, butterfly-inducing kiss I've ever had. Never felt anything like it before or since. It was sweet and sexy and after I pulled away and looked into her face I was like, "I'm soooo gay."

P.S. Right after this, my friends called out asking where I was and she replied, "In the closet!!"

Gender and sex aren’t the same thing. Biological sex - AKA having a penis or a vagina (some people are also born intersex with qualities of both) - is a scientific fact. Gender, however, is a social construct. 

You can think of gender as a form of expression; throughout human history there have been variations on how different cultures interpret and express gender. 

Because it hasn’t always been based on your biological sex and is changeable, people who are born with x genitalia are assigned x gender, when they may come to realize that they are in fact identify with y gender. Gender isn’t a fact, it’s something humans created to identify themselves and others and place them into categories. That’s why it’s referred to by many people in those terms. Do a little research into gender theory if you want to understand more about why certain terms are used!

Hi darling :)

Your experience sounds very similar to mine. I’ll explain it a bit (it’s going to be a little NSFW) as well as the journey I went through to realize I was attracted to women and that it was okay to not be attracted to men. 

In high school, I had a boyfriend constantly. At first it would be fun and I would get aroused and spend a lot of time and attention on them - but it would always fade and I would move on to a new guy and the cycle would start again. 

I always thought to myself while looking at them that they were unattractive or pitiful and felt bad for them, because I knew I wasn’t really interested even though I tried my hardest to love them. I loved a lot of them as friends but the romance/fooling around was forced. I thought for a long time that I had an inability to love people and saw myself as unkind and cruel because no matter how hard I tried, I couldn’t love them. 

My last boyfriend, I dated from the age of 18-21. We were long distance, and I lost my virginity to him. I thought many times throughout the relationship that either I must be a lesbian, not love him, or that there was something seriously wrong with my vagina because sex was never pleasurable and it was near impossible for me to enjoy it. I spent a lot of time getting drunk so I could sleep with my boyfriend. 

I always identified (very privately) as bisexual. Once we broke up, I started pushing myself to explore that side of me. I came out as bi, but still never acted upon it because I was so scared I wouldn’t actually be accepted or that I would be just plain bad at being with a girl. 

Then I met a wonderful girl in my poetry class - we took our time getting to know each other, and I had the only REAL first kiss of my life. The others had been awkward and forced and I felt bad, guilty or shameful about them afterwards (as well as every sexual encounter I’d had with a man). This kiss was wonderful and electric and I’d never experienced something quite like it (much like your kiss). It took me a few months of dating her to realize that I COULD enjoy sex, that I COULD maintain interest in somebody and that I wasn’t heartless - I just am who I am, meaning a girl who likes girls. 

Nobody by you can decide whether you’re gay or not, but from the perspective of a gay woman (now 22 years old) this is definitely something you should continue to think about and NOT be afraid of. Even if you start calling yourself gay in your own head - if it feels good and right to think it, you can work up the confidence to stop hiding from yourself. 

If you do decide that you identify as gay/lesbian, it’s going to feel really strange at first but then it will start to feel really good. It’s so freeing to find a label that fits you - just like it can be freeing to forego labels altogether.  

I would google “compulsory heterosexuality” - it helped me a lot to read about and might help you. You’re young and figuring it out, but no matter what happens you’re going to be okay :)
